abstract: Health programmes must clear cost-effectiveness thresholds, but social care faces no such test. This column uses Spain's 2007 long-term care reform to show that access to cash subsidies and publicly funded home help raised life satisfaction, reduced loneliness, and increased survival, at a cost per quality-adjusted life year well below the thresholds applied to health programmes. The results suggest that part of a national care service could be funded by replacing less cost-effective health programmes with social care.
authors: Joan Costa-i-Font, Sergi Jiménez-Martín, Cristina Vilaplana Prieto
title: Adult social care can be better value than the health care we already fund

abstract: Agreements between manufacturers and retailers can affect competition across brands and stores. This column documents retail price patterns in the US consumer battery industry and uses a model estimated from purchase data to explore two potential mechanisms: changes in downstream retail pricing and changes in upstream wholesale contracting. Counterfactual simulations illustrate how these mechanisms could jointly weaken competition. In the scenarios examined, the wholesale channel generates the larger consumer welfare loss. The findings highlight the importance of considering both channels when evaluating the potential effects of vertical agreements.
title: How agreements between suppliers and retailers can weaken competition

abstract: This paper studies patterns of functional change, defined as the change in the value chain functions performed within the manufacturing sector and related business services. To this end, a novel measure for the sophistication of value chain functions, labelled FUNCY, is developed, establishing a hierarchy of value chain functions. From the FUNCY measure functional productivities in the manufacturing sector are derived. A decomposition analysis, comprising developing and developed countries over time (2003-2022), suggests that, in contrast to the well-studied phenomenon of structural change, developing countries experienced modest functional upgrading over the past two decades. These group-level results mask large heterogeneity in the functional change component at the country level. Functional upgrading is driven by shifts from fabrication activities towards value chain functions with higher functional productivity such as business services. However, ‘large jumps’ to high-productivity functions such as ICT services or R&D activities are extremely rare.
title: Functional Upgrading in Global Value Chains
